title: Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis
authors: Bosquet L, Montpetit J, Arvisais D, Mujika I
journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise
population: Competitive athletes in taper interventions with field or competition performance outcomes (27 studies)
findings: 27 of 182 potential studies met inclusion criteria; six databases searched; outcome was pre-post standardized mean difference in performance.
Optimal taper duration was 2 weeks (overall effect = 0.59 +/- 0.33, P < 0.001).
Exponentially decreasing training volume by 41-60% gave the largest effect (overall effect = 0.72 +/- 0.36, P < 0.001).

Training intensity left unmodified (overall effect = 0.33 +/- 0.14, P < 0.001) and training frequency left unmodified (overall effect = 0.35 +/- 0.17, P < 0.001) were associated with performance gains.
limitations: Pooled across sports and competitive levels; the abstract gives no ultra-distance or recreational-runner subgroup and no participant total; pre-post effects weighted by within-group heterogeneity; components of the taper (duration, volume, pattern) were analysed as separate independent variables so their effects may be confounded (inference).
implications: Default taper for 5 km to marathon: 14 days, with average weekly volume reduced 41-60% relative to pre-taper volume.
Use a progressive/exponential decay rather than a single step; the exact weekly split is an engine design choice not stated in the abstract.
Keep intensity (pace of quality sessions) and run frequency unchanged during the taper; reduce volume by shortening runs rather than dropping sessions or lowering pace.

verification.notes: Crossref: 'Effects of Tapering on Performance', MSSE Aug 2007, Bosquet first author. All numbers re-checked in Europe PMC abstract (PMID 17762369). Researcher's population details (swimming, running, cycling, triathlon) and 'mostly trained to elite' are not in the abstract and were removed.
